defaults.permitted_development: In Scotland the main permitted development routes are a single-storey ground floor extension, a rear ground floor extension of more than one storey and certain roof enlargements. Each route has its own limits and none should be assumed in a conservation area.

rules.height_rules: Single-storey ground floor extensions should have eaves at or below 3m and overall height at or below 4m, with parts within 1m of a boundary no higher than 2.5m. More-than-one-storey rear extensions should not be higher than the existing house.
rules.depth_rules: Single-storey rear projection is up to 3m on a terraced house or 4m on other houses. More-than-one-storey rear extensions are a separate and tighter route, generally to the rear only, with a footprint no larger than the original dwellinghouse.
rules.boundary_rules: More-than-one-storey rear extensions should be at least 10m from the curtilage boundary. Single-storey work should not project forward of the principal elevation or a side elevation that fronts a road.
rules.roof_rules: Roof enlargements are a separate route and should not be assumed to make a front-facing dormer lawful. Check the specific roof-enlargement rules where the extension uses the roof.
rules.materials_rules: Use materials and detailing that sit appropriately with the existing house.

restrictions.conservation_area: In Scotland these householder extension rights do not apply in conservation areas. Treat written authority confirmation or a formal planning application as necessary before starting work.
restrictions.listed_building: Do not rely on permitted development for a listed building or its curtilage. Listed building consent is usually required for works affecting character, and planning permission may also be needed.

rules.permitted_development: Scottish householder PD is split into separate routes rather than one broad England-style Class A rule. The relevant extension route depends on whether the work is single-storey, a rear upper-floor addition or a roof enlargement.

rules.height_rules: Height control is stricter near the boundary in Scotland. Single-storey work should stay within 3m eaves and 4m overall height, dropping to 2.5m within 1m of a boundary, while rear upper floors stay below the existing house.
rules.depth_rules: Single-storey rear projection is up to 3m on a terraced house or 4m on other houses. More-than-one-storey rear extensions are a separate and tighter route, generally to the rear only, with a footprint no larger than the original dwellinghouse.
rules.boundary_rules: Boundary and frontage position are the key Scottish tests. Rear upper floors should keep 10m from the curtilage boundary, while single-storey work should stay behind the principal elevation and any side elevation facing a road.
rules.roof_rules: Roof enlargements are a separate route and should not be assumed to make a front-facing dormer lawful. Check the specific roof-enlargement rules where the extension uses the roof.
rules.materials_rules: Choose wall, roof and joinery finishes that tie the extension back to the existing house so the addition reads as one building.

rules.permitted_development: A house extension may fall within Scottish permitted development rights, but only where it fits the correct Scottish route for the form proposed and avoids the conservation-area restrictions.

rules.materials_rules: Use materials that closely relate to the existing house. Extensions are easier to justify where they look integrated rather than obviously added on.
